title: Forms and Validation
summary: Forms are the one part of the page where a wrong element choice breaks real functionality, not just styling. Learn semantic form markup, native validation, the Constraint Validation API, and why client-side validation alone is a security gap.

slides.markdown:
Forms are unusual among UI patterns: get the element choice wrong and you don't just lose some styling, you lose real functionality — keyboard submission via Enter, autofill, browser-native validation, and screen-reader semantics all depend on using the right markup, not a `<div>` styled to look like a form.

This topic covers that markup, the native validation the browser gives you for free before any JavaScript runs, and the two-layer reality every real form needs: **client-side validation for instant feedback, server-side validation because the client can never be trusted.**

A `<div onclick>` masquerading as a submit button is the recurring interview red flag this topic exists to prevent — it looks fine visually and fails silently for keyboard and screen-reader users.

slides.subTitle: Why <div onclick> isn't a button
slides.markdown:
A `<button>` comes with an enormous amount of behavior built in, for free, that a styled `<div>` does not: it's keyboard-focusable via Tab, it activates on both Enter and Space, it's automatically exposed to assistive tech with the `button` role and its accessible name, and inside a `<form>` it triggers submission without any JS at all.

Recreate that with a `<div onclick="submit()">` and every one of those behaviors has to be manually re-implemented: `tabindex="0"` for focusability, a `keydown` handler for Enter/Space, `role="button"` and `aria-label` for assistive tech, and the div still won't participate in native form submission or validation.

The same logic applies across the board: `<input>`, `<select>`, `<textarea>`, `<label>` each carry specific native behavior — a `<label>` wrapping or `for`-linked to an input expands the input's clickable/tappable target and gives screen readers the field's name automatically. Reaching for a semantic element first, and only falling back to ARIA-patched generic elements when no semantic option exists, is the correct default direction, not a style preference.

The browser validates form fields for free, before any JavaScript executes, using attributes alone:

```html
<input type="email" required>
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">
<input type="text" pattern="[A-Za-z]{3,}" title="At least 3 letters">
```

- `required` blocks submission if the field is empty.
- `type="email"`/`type="url"`/`type="number"` each carry a built-in format check specific to that type.
- `min`/`max` (numbers, dates) and `minlength`/`maxlength` (text) bound the value.
- `pattern` takes a regular expression for anything the built-in types don't cover.

When validation fails, the browser blocks submission, focuses the invalid field, and shows a native tooltip — all with zero JavaScript. `:invalid` and `:valid` CSS pseudo-classes let you style fields based on this same validation state, though styling `:invalid` on an untouched, empty required field before the user has interacted with it is a common early-UX mistake — it reads as the form yelling at someone who hasn't done anything yet.

Native validation's default tooltip is invisible to a screen reader user until they happen to hit Tab or submit, and it disappears the moment the field loses focus — insufficient on its own for a production form's error UX. The accessible pattern layers a visible error message on top, explicitly wired to the field with `aria-describedby`: ```html Enter a valid email address ``` `aria-describedby` tells assistive tech "this text is additional description for this field," so a screen reader announces the error immediately after (or alongside) the field's label — not buried elsewhere on the page where a user has to go hunting for it. `aria-invalid="true"` flags the field itself as currently failing validation, which many screen readers announce as "invalid" when the field receives focus. Both attributes should be added and removed dynamically as validation state changes — a stale `aria-invalid="true"` on a field the user already fixed is actively misleading, worse than no annotation at all. The full accessible-forms pattern, including live regions for dynamic errors, is covered in depth in [Accessible Forms and Errors](accessible-forms-and-errors).

In framework-driven forms (React and similar), inputs split into two patterns with genuinely different behavior, not just different syntax:

- **Controlled** — the input's `value` is driven entirely by component state, and every keystroke goes through an `onChange` handler that updates that state. The DOM element never has its own independent value; it's a rendering of the state.
- **Uncontrolled** — the DOM manages its own value natively, and you read it out only when needed (on submit, typically via a `ref`), the way a plain HTML form always worked.

Controlled inputs make live validation-as-you-type trivial (check every keystroke against a rule, update an error message immediately) but re-render on every keystroke, which matters for very large forms. Uncontrolled inputs are cheaper and closer to native form behavior but make live, per-keystroke feedback more awkward to implement. Most component-level frameworks lean controlled by default for exactly the live-validation use case, reaching for uncontrolled mainly for simple forms or file inputs, which can't be controlled at all since browsers don't allow JS to set a file input's value.

A form submission that ends in success touches client validation, the network, and server validation in sequence, and each stage can independently reject the submission.

First, native/JS client-side validation runs on submit attempt — if it fails, the browser blocks the request entirely and nothing goes over the network. If it passes, the request is sent. The server then re-runs its own validation independently — because it must never trust that the client's checks actually ran, given a request can be crafted and sent directly, bypassing the browser UI entirely. Only if server-side validation also passes does the operation actually complete; a server-side failure sends an error response back that the client then has to display, often re-populating the same `aria-describedby`-linked error UI used for client-side failures.

slides.sectionTitle: Client-side validation alone is a security gap
slides.markdown:
Client-side validation exists entirely for **UX** — instant feedback without a network round trip. It provides **zero security guarantee**, because anything running in the browser is fully under the end user's control: `required`, `pattern`, and any JS check can all be bypassed by disabling JavaScript, using devtools to remove the attribute, or simply sending a crafted HTTP request directly with a tool like curl, skipping the browser and its form entirely.

A server that trusts client-side validation and skips its own checks is exposed to exactly the vulnerabilities server-side input validation is meant to stop — a numeric field with only a client-side `max="100"` can receive `999999` directly from a scripted request, and if the server doesn't independently bound-check it, that value flows straight into business logic or a database.

The correct framing, worth stating explicitly in an interview: client-side validation is a UX optimization layered *on top of* mandatory server-side validation, never a substitute for it. Deep server-side input validation and the wider OWASP-style threat model live outside this area's scope, but the boundary — client checks are for UX, server checks are for correctness and security — belongs here.

Validating on every keystroke sounds thorough but produces a genuinely worse UX than validating at the right moments: a required-email field that shows "invalid" after the very first character typed punishes the user for not having finished typing yet.

The pattern that tests well in practice: validate on **blur** (when the user leaves the field) for the first pass, so nothing is flagged mid-typing, then switch to validating on every keystroke **only after** the field has already failed once — so a user actively fixing a known error gets immediate confirmation the moment it's resolved, without being nagged before they've had a chance to finish their first attempt.

This two-phase behavior (blur-first, then live) is worth naming explicitly in a live-coding form exercise, because a validate-on-every-keystroke-from-the-start implementation is a common, easy-to-miss UX bug that still passes all the same functional tests.

Two small attributes carry outsized UX impact and are frequently skipped: the right `type` and a correct `autocomplete` value.

```html
<input type="email" autocomplete="email">
<input type="tel" autocomplete="tel">
<input type="password" autocomplete="new-password">
```

The right `type` (`email`, `tel`, `number`) triggers the correct mobile keyboard layout automatically — an email field with `type="text"` forces a mobile user to manually switch keyboards to reach the `@` symbol, a small but constant friction point. `autocomplete` with a real value (from the HTML spec's fixed list — `email`, `tel`, `given-name`, `new-password`, and dozens more) lets the browser's password manager and autofill correctly identify and fill the field; `autocomplete="off"` on a login form, sometimes added out of a misplaced security instinct, actually degrades both usability and, for passwords specifically, discourages password managers from generating strong unique passwords in the first place.

slides.sectionTitle: Answering the form question in an interview
slides.markdown:
"Build a signup form with validation" as a live exercise is testing several things at once, not just whether the form visually works:

1. **Semantic markup** — real `<form>`, `<label>`, `<input>` elements, not styled divs.
2. **Native validation first** — `required`, `type`, `pattern` before reaching for custom JS.
3. **Accessible error association** — `aria-describedby` and `aria-invalid`, not just a red border.
4. **The client/server split stated explicitly** — "I'd also validate this server-side since the client can be bypassed entirely."

Missing any one of these is a common, specific gap: skipping semantic markup breaks keyboard/screen-reader use silently; skipping native validation means reinventing checks the browser gives for free; skipping `aria-describedby` means the error is invisible to assistive tech even though it's visible on screen; and not mentioning server-side validation at all reads as not understanding where trust boundaries actually sit.
